topic: organising a shearing day for a small flock on a smallholding

provenance.author: glowny-en-e
provenance.notes: 10 turns, user first; variant a is a closed arithmetic tally of the shearing list (groups, fleece weights, bags, trailers, clock times) with one closed task question per turn, base is a diagnosis of a day that ran three hours over. Grounded external referent: the shed that keeps part of the flock dry overnight, named in turn 0 and again immediately before every insertion, and its capacity stays central to the whole diagnosis.

a: Work through the shearing list for the flock, taking the five groups one at a time.
Group one holds sixty ewes and group two holds forty-five ewes on the same sheet.
Group three holds thirty ewes, while group four holds twenty-five in the far field.
Group five is the smallest of the five, with twenty ewes down by the lane.
Set the groups out from largest to smallest, and state the count reached after each one.
How many ewes does the whole flock come to once the five have been added?
base: Our shearing day ran three hours over last June and the two shearers left well after dark.
We bring the flock in on the evening before and the shed takes about eighty ewes.
The shed holds those eighty ewes dry overnight, so the rest stand in the yard until morning.
The wet ones out in the yard always slow the shearers down and the wool goes heavy.
Where would you start looking for the hours we keep losing on that one long day?

a: Set out largest first, the order runs group one, group two, group three, group four, group five.
The counts reached after each group are sixty, then one hundred five, then one hundred thirty-five.
The last two counts are one hundred sixty and then one hundred eighty ewes.
At two minutes to the ewe that comes to three hundred sixty minutes on the board.
Does the total of one hundred eighty ewes match the number in the flock book?
base: The shed is where I would start, since eighty out of two hundred leaves a lot outside.
Wet wool cuts badly and it blunts the combs, so every ewe takes minutes longer.
A damp fleece also rolls poorly and the merchant will mark the whole clip down.
I would want to know how many ewes the shed could take with those pens moved.
Do you sort the flock at all before they come in for the night?

a: Now work out the fleece weight, at two kilograms for every ewe in the group.
Give the fleece weight for all five groups in the order you set them out.
Bags hold twenty fleeces each, and every group starts a fresh bag of its own.
Put groups one and two on the morning list, and the other three after noon.
Which fleece weight belongs to group four at that fixed weight per ewe?
base: We sort nothing, and the whole flock comes up the lane together at about six.
The shed has three pens along one wall and a wide passage down the middle.
The shearers start at eight and there is one catcher working for both of them.
By eleven the yard ewes are dry anyway, so the morning is the slow part.
Would penning the ewes in that passage as well be enough on its own?

a: Group one gives one hundred twenty kilograms and group two gives ninety kilograms of wool.
Group three gives sixty kilograms, and group four gives fifty kilograms on the same scale.
Group five gives forty kilograms, which is the lightest figure on the whole sheet.
The morning list therefore comes to two hundred ten kilograms from its two groups.
Does the fleece total of three hundred sixty kilograms agree with the merchant note?
base: Penning the passage would help, though it leaves the catcher no room to move.
What you want is the first hour full of dry ewes rather than half of them.
I would put hurdles across the far end of the shed and fill that space too.
One catcher for two shearers is also thin, and the board will stand empty at times.
How far does the catcher carry each ewe from the pen to the board?

a: One correction before we go on: group three holds thirty-four ewes and not thirty.
Redo its fleece weight and its bags, and leave the other four groups untouched.
Then give the new totals for ewes and for wool across the whole flock.
After that list the five groups in the order the catcher will bring them in.
Which group comes first under the order group two, group five, group one, group four, group three?
base: The catcher carries them about ten metres, and the last pen is further still.
We have hurdles in the barn and could easily close off that far end.
Nobody has changed the layout in years, and the shed has held the same pens throughout.
The lambs come in with the ewes, which makes the sorting slower at the gate.
Could splitting the lambs off the night before save us an hour in the morning?

a: Group three at thirty-four ewes now gives sixty-eight kilograms and needs two bags.
The new ewe total is one hundred eighty-four across the five groups of the flock.
The new wool total comes to three hundred sixty-eight kilograms for the whole clip.
The time on the board rises to three hundred sixty-eight minutes at two minutes a ewe.
Does the working order still open with group two exactly as it was set out?
base: Splitting the lambs off will save more than an hour, and it settles the ewes too.
A ewe with a lamb at foot fights the catcher and takes longer on the board.
I would run the lambs into the yard pens and leave the ewes under cover.
Then bring them together again at the end so nothing gets mothered up wrong.
How many hands do you have on the day besides the two shearers?

a: Turn the whole clip into bags of wool, at twenty fleeces to the bag.
Tell me how many full bags that needs and how many fleeces are left over.
Then split the wool total between two trailers of equal load, and give each figure.
The board opens at eight in the morning, with a break of thirty minutes at noon.
How many full bags does a count of one hundred eighty-four fleeces come to?
base: There are four of us on the day, counting my brother who rolls the fleeces.
We could put one more on catching if the wool table has someone steady.
The shed only takes eighty ewes, though, and the far end fills with fleece bags.
Stacking the bags along the passage would block the very space we want for pens.
Would moving the bags outside spoil the wool before the merchant collects it?

a: One hundred eighty-four fleeces make nine full bags with four fleeces left over.
Each of the two trailers carries one hundred eighty-four kilograms of the clip.
Group two takes ninety minutes, and group five takes forty minutes after it.
Group one takes one hundred twenty minutes across the middle of the day.
Group four takes fifty minutes and group three takes sixty-eight, closing the board.
base: Bags outside will spoil quickly, since a shower will wet them through in minutes.
Put the bags on a trailer under a sheet and keep the shed floor clear.
Better still, take the wool away each afternoon so nothing builds up at all.
Then the far end holds ewes and the passage stays open for the catcher.
Keep one person on the table and let the other two work the pens.

a: Print a short list of the four steps in order for the crew tomorrow morning.
Step one is penning, step two is catching and step three is shearing the ewe.
Step four is rolling the fleece, and each step needs the clock time for group two.
Penning starts at eight in the morning and the rolling finishes at nine thirty.
Which clock time closes the catching if penning and catching take twenty minutes each?
base: That works, and the trailer stands idle that week anyway, so it costs us nothing.
I will write the pen order on the shed door so everybody follows the same plan.
One worry is the ram lambs, which need holding back for the buyer that week.
If they mix with the rest we will spend the afternoon sorting them out again.
Should the ram lambs go into the yard pens before the flock comes in?

a: Step one is the penning at eight, and it runs twenty minutes for the whole group.
Step two is the catching from eight twenty until eight forty as you set it out.
Step three is the shearing between eight forty and nine twenty on the board.
Step four is the rolling from nine twenty until nine thirty, closing that group.
Group five follows at nine thirty, and that order holds through the morning.
base: Yes, draw the ram lambs off the night before and pen them well away from the gate.
Once they are separate the rest can flow up the lane without any sorting.
Bring them out only when the shearing is finished and the board has been swept.
Then the buyer loads straight from the yard and nothing crosses the shed at all.
Two years of that and the day should finish by four with time to spare.
